Book Review
RomantasyDark FantasyGrimdark

Alchemised

by SenLinYu
★★★★★

"Alchemised is brutal, morally grey grimdark done right, using its unflinching darkness to explore religious manipulation, gendered violence, and the immigrant experience without ever feeling gratuitous. Anchored by a meticulously detailed magic system and a devastating slow-burn romance between Helena and Kaine, it's an unforgettable 5-star read.

SenLinYu·December 2025

am a huge fan of dark fantasy and the grimdark genre. The darker, grimmer, and more emotionally punishing a story is, the more I tend to enjoy it. Before reading Alchemised, I had never heard of the author, and only after finishing did I learn that this was their debut novel. I also found out that Alchemised originally began as a Harry Potter fanfiction titled Manacled. I do read fanfiction occasionally, but I am not part of the Harry Potter fandom and have no desire to join it. From what I understand, the author reworked and transformed the original setting into a new world with new lore. I am glad I read Alchemised first. I do not plan to read the fanfiction version because the fandom itself does not appeal to me.

Before going further, a small disclaimer. There will be spoilers.

And most importantly, do not read this book if you are sensitive to any of the following: rape and sexual assault, necrophilia, torture, wartime violence, religious abuse, systemic oppression, complex trauma, suicidal ideation, self harm, PTSD, medical torture, eugenics, cannibalism, death, or extremely graphic gore. Nothing is softened. Everything is described in visceral detail.

You might now ask yourself, why read something like this? Is it misery for the sake of misery? Is it grimdark without meaning? For me, the answer is no. The darkness here serves a purpose. Alchemised is brutal, but it uses its brutality to explore themes that are powerful, thought provoking, and emotionally resonant. This book is not simply dark. It has something to say.

One of its greatest strengths is the morally grey nature of every character and faction. There is no purely good side. Even Helena, our main character, sometimes forces you to question whether you should root for her. On one side is the Guild, which claims to value democracy and progress, yet it is loyal to Morrough, the most powerful necromancer alive. They practice necromancy, torture, cannibalism, and medical experimentation. The necrothralls they create are described in horrifying sensory detail. You smell the rot. You see the decay. The descriptions of these abominations are vivid enough to make you sick.

On the other side is the Order of the Eternal Flame. They follow strict religious doctrine and are blinded by fanaticism. Their rigid principles ultimately contribute to their downfall. What makes their depiction especially compelling is how the author explores religious manipulation. The leaders twist faith into a tool for control. They convince the Resistance to interpret small victories as “miracles” or “favors” from Sol. They preach purity and obedience as the only path to survival. Meanwhile, they privately acknowledge that none of this is true. Their authority rests entirely on keeping their followers ignorant and unquestioning.

These are supposed to be the good guys. Yet they view women as lesser. Their voices are silenced. Their work is undervalued. Their agency is consistently stripped away. Even Helena, one of their most talented healers, is forced to choose between being sterilized in order to serve or preserving her ability to have children. The fact that this is presented as a choice tells you everything about women’s status in this society. Meanwhile, women on the Guild’s side often hold positions of power, but even they face unimaginable consequences if captured. The book does not hide the gendered nature of wartime violence.

The immigrant experience is another theme woven deeply into the narrative. Helena is not from the kingdom where the story takes place. In the flashbacks that dominate Part Two, we see her struggle to belong in a society that sees her as an outsider. The early chapters of Part Two highlight how she is treated differently, distrusted, and underestimated. This shapes her compassion, her determination, and her overwhelming desire to help others, even when those same people despise her.

And then we come to the world itself. This world is suffocatingly dark. Necrothralls roam freely. Towns and cities crumble under constant war. Hope is a rare luxury. Yet in the middle of all this bleakness, a sincere and beautiful romance develops. Two broken, lonely people who have nothing find solace in each other. Their relationship is written with care, authenticity, and emotional depth. Even though they belong to opposing factions, they always look out for each other, no matter the risk.

When I first started reading, Helena’s early interactions with Kaine honestly made me feel sick. I knew the book contained romance, but I kept thinking there was no way Kaine could be the love interest. He seemed too cruel, too cold, too far gone. Then Part Two begins. Helena falls into a coma, and through her memories we are transported to the early days of the war. This is where everything changes.

We see who Kaine used to be. We witness the moment that shattered him. After his mother’s death, which he blames entirely on the Guild and on Morrough, he begins secretly providing information to the Resistance. He never officially joins them, but he risks himself to help in the only way he can. From here, his relationship with Helena blossoms slowly and painfully. By the time we return to the present in Part Three, everything about Kaine’s character suddenly makes sense. Every contradiction, every harsh action, every emotional fragment becomes understandable. Their love endures trauma, war, betrayal, and suffering. Helena fights for the ones she loves and Kaine fights for the one person who still loves him.

The side characters deserve special recognition. Each one feels distinct and meaningful. The romance subplot between Luc and Lilia is a touching and tragic addition. Their dynamic adds emotional variety and makes the world feel more alive. The twist before Luc’s death is devastating and shines a spotlight on the ideological roots of the conflict.

Now, the worldbuilding. This is where the book truly excels. The author does not overwhelm readers with dense exposition. Instead, they reveal lore in small, perfectly timed pieces, allowing the reader to absorb the world naturally. The atmosphere is rich and oppressive. You can feel the tension in every environment. The way necromancy, religion, politics, and war interlock creates a world that feels terrifyingly real.

The magic system is a standout feature. It is a detailed hard magic system with clear rules, limitations, and consequences. Healing magic, necromancy, and more experimental forms all feel grounded in biological and chemical logic. The descriptions of magical processes often resemble medical procedures. If you enjoy scientific or medical worldbuilding, you will love this aspect. It genuinely feels like the author has a background in biology.

Alchemy is also woven throughout the magic system. I was originally biased against alchemy in fantasy because it often feels vague or symbolic. Here, however, it is handled with precision and creativity. Alchemical transmutations, metallic properties, and chemical reactions are integrated into the magic in a way that feels tangible. Readers who enjoy the material and scientific side of fantasy will be especially delighted.

The only drawback here is that the terminology can feel overwhelming at first. There are many new words and concepts introduced quickly. A glossary or terminology list at the end would have made the first few chapters smoother. Once you adjust, however, the system becomes one of the most rewarding aspects of the book.

Despite this minor criticism, Alchemised is an extraordinary grimdark novel. It is brutal, emotional, and fearless in its exploration of trauma, faith, and survival. It breaks its characters, rebuilds them, and forces you to confront the worst parts of humanity alongside them. Yet in the middle of all this darkness, it manages to find love, resilience, and meaning.

This book stayed with me long after I finished it. For readers who appreciate morally grey worlds, complex characters, and grimdark themes, Alchemised is unforgettable.

My rating is an easy 5 out of 5.

By Ruşen M. Özoruç
